//coverImage: The manuscript ships no cover photograph — only a portrait TOPIC 2 infographic on a cream ground, which cannot sit in the landscape hero window without being cut, and which left broad empty cream bands when it was padded to fit. So the hero is built rather than fitted: four of the manuscript’s own pictures as a full-bleed 2x2 mosaic at exactly 2474x1340 = the window’s 144:78 at 436 DPI for its 144mm printed width, so the pictures reach all four edges and the engine crops nothing. The four are chosen for what they show as well as for quality: between them they carry a wheelchair user, an albino learner and a blind man with a white cane, and the people counted across all four are close to evenly male and female (house rule: every picture with people in it, the cover included). Each cell keeps a 144:78 band chosen so no face is cut; the ambitions picture is additionally cropped past its lettered chalkboard and above its DREAM PLAN card, because a cover carries no half-read lettering. At the centre is Zambia — the outline traced from the Geography Form 1 book’s population map (the border only, none of that map’s labels, colours or legend) in the theme’s gold on its indigo, ringed by the four religions the RE syllabus teaches: the cross, the star and crescent, om and the Baha’i nine-pointed star. OUTSTANDING: the four photographs are not themselves religious. The manuscript contains no picture of worship, scripture or religious life in any of the four religions — its 18 pictures are lettered infographics about forgiveness, justice, ethics and hope plus these four scenes — so a cover whose PICTURES depict the subject needs new artwork generated (see docs/HOUSE-STYLE.md §5 on gpt-image-2).
//authors: The manuscript's cover byline is one 44-character string ('Francis Siakumena and Mirriam Mhone-Muzona'), which the cover's author filter drops as too long, leaving only the name recovered from the AUTHORS bio section. Split into two so the cover reads AUTHORS and credits both. The second name is spelled WITHOUT the hyphen the manuscript uses — Mirriam Mhone Muzona — on the author's own instruction.

BA-Primary is its own bold run, so the paragraph splits cleanly in front of it and the entry gets its own line.
//subtext: Round 2. Two standardisations the proofreader asked for and one spelling. (1) The line introducing each Specific Competence was written four different ways across the book's 22 sub-topics - 'In this sub-topic, you will:' 12 times, 'In this subtopic, you will:' 4, 'In this subtopic, you will learn to:' 4, 'In this sub-topic, you will learn to:' once, 'In this section, you will:' once. The notes 'let it be sub-topic' (page 2) and 'make this standard for all before the specific competences' (page 75) both point at it, so all 22 are normalised to the commonest form. The two other 'In this section, you will ...' sentences are running prose, not lead-ins, and are left alone. (2) 'rumors' -> 'rumours': the note reads 'delete and write like this; rumuors', which is a slip for the British spelling - the book already writes 'rumours' twice against 'rumors' twice, and is consistently -our/-ise throughout (behaviour 55, colour 48, recognise 31, and no American spelling anywhere). (4) The second author's name was printed three ways in one book: 'Mirriam Mhone Muzona' on the cover (set by the authors override, on her own instruction), 'Mirriam Mhone-Muzona' on the imprint page, and 'Mirriam Mhone\u2011Muzona' - with a non-breaking hyphen - in her own AUTHORS biography. The instruction had only ever reached the cover. Both hyphenated forms are now normalised to the spelling she asked for. (5) Spelling found at the pre-print check, none of it raised by the proofreader. The book is consistently British - behaviour 55, colour 48, recognise 31, organis- 26, apologis- 16 - but carried one 'apologize', one 'organizations', and used the American 'practicing/practice' for the VERB in four places against nine British 'practising'. The noun 'into practice' is correct and is left alone. The sentence ending '...the relationship between freedom and laws in the community' had no full stop, in both places it appears.

//removeRange: Round 2, printed pages 155-156: "Refer to the Learner's Book or attached Activity" and "Please get the right activity from the Learners' Book or the attached copy in word". No Word file was attached, but the manuscript answers the note itself. LEARNING ACTIVITY 18 is the one activity the writer drew no box border around, so the box ran on past the instruction and took in his planning scaffold: a bare list of scripture references under "1. Christianity", "2. Hindu", "3. Muslim" and "4. Zambian Traditional Religion", a "Discussion Task" repeating word for word the instruction six lines above it, and the unfinished note to himself "Also add appropriate proverbs ...". Immediately below the box the same sub-topic sets all of it out as finished learner prose, religion by religion. So the scaffold goes, from "1. Christianity" to the end of the box, leaving the activity as its instruction alone - the shape the proofreader asked for on the other sixty activities. Three teachings in the scaffold were NOT repeated in the prose and are carried into it by the edits below, so nothing is lost.
//edit: The three teachings the scaffold removed above carried alone, written into the prose in the author's own words. (1) Bhagavad Gita 3:8 was the only scriptural reference for Hinduism anywhere in the sub-topic - the Hindu prose cites none, while Christianity carries five references, Islam carries Qur'an 53:39 and Zambian Traditional Religion carries proverbs. (2) "Work is a command" is Islam's framing of work as an obligation rather than a choice; the prose says work is valuable and should be honest but never that it is commanded, and the scaffold's own contrast line ("emphasis on divine command, communal duty, or personal motives") points straight back at it. (3) "Neglecting work results in lack of food" is the Zambian Traditional Religion consequence; the prose covers responsibility, communal work and cooperation but never what follows from not working.

edit.find: This encourages you to take pride in doing your duties well.
edit.with: This encourages you to take pride in doing your duties well. Bhagavad Gita 3:8 teaches that performing your duty is better than avoiding work. This encourages you to take part in your responsibilities rather than leaving them to others.

edit.find: Islam recognises the dignity of people who work with their hands and encourages respect for manual workers.
edit.with: Work is regarded as a command rather than a matter of personal choice. Islam recognises the dignity of people who work with their hands and encourages respect for manual workers.

edit.find: A person is expected to contribute according to their abilities and circumstances rather than remaining unwilling to help others.
edit.with: A person is expected to contribute according to their abilities and circumstances rather than remaining unwilling to help others. Neglecting work is discouraged because it can result in a lack of food and hardship for the family.
